easy.heading: Warming Up With A Friendly Friday Grid
easy.body:
Happy Friday, everyone! I hope you have a cozy drink ready because today's Pips puzzle was such a treat. I started with the easy grid, and right away, my eyes jumped to that sum region in the top right corner. It needed three cells—(0,4), (1,4), and (2,4)—to add up to ten. Since I had a [5,5] domino in my tray, it felt like the perfect anchor. I placed the [5,5] at (0,4) and (1,4), which meant the last cell at (2,4) had to be a zero to keep the sum at ten.

From there, the bottom left gave me a huge hint with the greater than five rule at cell (3,0). Looking at my remaining pieces, the [6,0] domino was the only one that could satisfy that, so I tucked the 6 into (3,0) and the 0 into (2,0). This was great because it also checked off the empty constraint for (2,0). It is always so satisfying when two rules click together like that!

Finally, I had to deal with the equals region across the middle. Since I had a [3,3] and a [3,5] left, I realized that if I put the [3,3] at (1,0) and (1,1), and the 3-side of my [3,5] at (1,2), all three cells would equal three. That left the 5-side at (2,2) and the final [0,0] domino to fill in (2,3) and (2,4). Everything fit perfectly, and it was a great way to wake up my brain.

medium.heading: Navigating The Middle Of The Road
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today felt a bit more like a scavenger hunt. The first thing I noticed were those single-cell target regions. When you see a target sum of 6 at (2,3) and a target sum of 4 at (5,3), you know exactly what numbers need to go there. I looked at my dominoes and saw [3,4] and a couple of sixes in [0,6] and [6,6]. I held onto those for a second while I looked for a place to start building.

I decided to tackle the bottom half first. The equals region at (6,2) and (6,3) was a good clue, especially since it sat right below the sum of 4. By placing the [3,4] domino vertically at (4,3) and (5,3), I got my 4 in the right spot. Then, looking at the sum of 3 needed for (5,1) and (5,2), I used the [2,5] and [0,1] pieces to balance things out. It took a little bit of shuffling, but once the bottom was set, the top fell into place.

What really helped me finish was the equals constraint at (0,0), (1,0), and (1,1). I had the [5,5] and [6,6] dominoes left, and by placing them carefully, I was able to make sure those three cells all shared the same value. The medium level always tests my patience with those small overlapping areas, but it felt so good to see the whole board turn green!

hard.heading: Tackling The Big Sum Six Challenge
hard.body:
Wow, Rodolfo Kurchan really brought the heat today! This hard puzzle was basically a giant puzzle of sixes. Almost every single constraint was a sum of 6, which actually helps once you realize you are looking for specific pairs. I started by identifying all the single-cell regions that had to be 6, like (0,1), (6,1), (6,5), and (7,5). Once I knew those cells had to be sixes, I looked at which dominoes in my tray actually had a 6 on them, like [0,6], [2,6], [6,1], and [5,6].

One of the trickiest parts was the large region in the middle spanning (3,4), (3,5), (4,4), and (4,5) that had to sum to 6. With four cells to work with, there were a few ways to do it, but I had to save my bigger numbers for the single-cell spots. I ended up using smaller values like ones and twos there. It felt like a delicate balancing act! I actually hit a dead end halfway through because I used the [0,6] domino too early in the top corner, but once I swapped it for the [6,1], the rest of the path cleared up.

Cruising through the finish line involved double-checking the equals region at (3,1) and (4,1). I used the [3,3] domino there, which helped satisfy the sum of 6 for the neighboring cells at (3,0) and (4,0). It is rare to see a puzzle where one number is so dominant, but it made for a really unique solving experience today. If you got stuck, don't feel bad—this one was a real brain teaser!

explanation.tips: Always start by looking for regions that consist of only a single cell, as these tell you exactly what number must go there. Also, try to identify which dominoes are unique, like a [6,6] or [0,0], because they have very limited places they can fit when sum constraints are involved. If you get stuck, try working from the corners inward, as they usually have the fewest possible combinations.
explanation.learned: Today's puzzles really showed me how a single repeated number can change the whole vibe of a grid. In the hard puzzle, the constant target of six meant I had to be extremely careful about where I placed my high-value dominoes early on. I also realized that equals regions are great for narrowing down which doubles, like [3,3] or [5,5], you should use versus using two different dominoes that happen to have the same number on one side.

faqs.question: How do I solve the NYT Pips puzzle for March 20?
faqs.answer: Focus on the target sum regions first. In the easy puzzle, use the [5,5] for the sum of 10. In the hard puzzle, identify all the cells that must be 6 due to the single-cell sum regions.

faqs.question: What does the Equals constraint mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: The Equals constraint means that all cells within that highlighted region must have the exact same number of pips.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for Hard Pips puzzles?
faqs.answer: Look for the most restrictive constraints. Single-cell sums or very small sums with large regions are the best places to start because they limit your domino choices significantly.

faqs.question: Can I reuse dominoes in the same Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: No, you can only use each domino provided in the tray once. If you find yourself needing a piece you already placed, you'll need to rethink your previous moves!

faqs.question: What does a Greater Than region mean?
faqs.answer: A Greater Than region (like the one in today's Easy puzzle) means the sum of the pips in that region must be higher than the target number shown.
